name: Family-Based Treatment (FBT)
summary: Family-Based Treatment (FBT) is a structured, caregiver-led therapy used mainly for children and adolescents with anorexia nervosa (and sometimes bulimia nervosa) to restore safe eating and reduce eating-disorder behaviors with active family support.
description: Family-Based Treatment (FBT), sometimes called the Maudsley approach, is a manualized outpatient therapy where parents or caregivers take an active, practical role in helping a young person eat enough and interrupt eating-disorder behaviors. The therapist coaches the family to support consistent nutrition, reduce symptoms, and gradually hand control of eating back to the adolescent as health and stability improve. FBT is not a substitute for medical stabilization or emergency care, and it may not fit when home supervision is not possible or the family environment is unsafe.

delivery_methods: Teletherapy (when medically appropriate and family supervision is feasible)
metadata.training_required: Clinician training in FBT and eating-disorder risk management, ideally with supervision/consultation.
treatment_duration: Commonly delivered over 6–12 months depending on severity and service setting

primary_indications: Anorexia nervosa in children and adolescents
Bulimia nervosa in adolescents (in some settings)
contraindications: Medical instability requiring inpatient medical stabilization or a higher level of care
Unsafe home environment (violence, severe neglect, or active abuse) where meal support cannot be provided safely
Lack of an available caregiver to provide consistent supervision and meal support
Severe family conflict that prevents basic collaboration without additional interventions
clinical_metadata.safety_profile: Generally safe when matched to medical risk and paired with medical monitoring. Distress and conflict can increase early during meal support. Safety depends on clear escalation plans for medical or psychiatric deterioration.
clinical_metadata.evidence_level: Strong evidence supports FBT as a first-line outpatient treatment for adolescents with anorexia nervosa. Evidence also supports its use for adolescent bulimia nervosa, with outcomes depending on severity and engagement.
clinical_metadata.research_support: Randomized trials and guideline recommendations support FBT for adolescent anorexia nervosa, emphasizing early nutritional rehabilitation, interruption of eating-disorder behaviors, and caregiver involvement.

items: Eating disorders in children and adolescents

best_for: Children and adolescents with anorexia nervosa who can be treated safely as outpatients
Adolescents with bulimia nervosa when caregiver support is feasible and medically appropriate
Families who can provide consistent meal supervision and are willing to take an active role
Situations where rapid stabilization of eating behaviors is a priority
works_well_when: Medical monitoring is in place and outpatient safety criteria are met
At least one caregiver can reliably supervise meals and snacks
The family can align on a practical plan even if emotions run high
School and home schedules can support regular eating and follow-up visits
common_use_cases: Restrictive eating with weight loss or failure to gain expected weight in youth
Meal avoidance, rituals, and fear of weight gain that block normal eating
Early-stage eating disorder where fast interruption of behaviors matters
Bulimic behaviors in adolescents when caregiver structure reduces binge–purge cycles

not_a_good_fit: Medical instability that requires inpatient stabilization or supervised refeeding
No available caregiver to provide meal support and supervision
Unsafe home environment where providing care would increase risk
Young people living independently without consistent support
use_with_extra_support: High suicide risk, self-harm risk, or severe comorbidity (may need coordinated psychiatry and a higher level of care)
Severe family conflict (may need additional family work or supports alongside FBT)
Autism traits, sensory sensitivities, or rigid routines (often needs individualized adaptations and extra coaching)
Ongoing purging or compulsive exercise (may need tighter monitoring and program-level support)
urgent_red_flags: Fainting, chest pain, confusion, severe weakness, or signs of dehydration
Inability to eat or drink enough daily, or rapid worsening of restriction
Uncontrolled purging, blood in vomit, or severe abdominal pain
Suicidal thoughts with intent or a plan
If any of these are present, seek urgent medical evaluation and contact local emergency services if immediate danger.

sections.text: FBT treats the eating disorder as the problem, not the child. Caregivers take temporary control of food and eating routines to restore medical and nutritional stability. As symptoms improve, control is gradually returned to the adolescent, and therapy then focuses on relapse prevention and age-appropriate development. The core mechanism is consistent, supported nutrition and interruption of eating-disorder behaviors, coached by a trained clinician.

steps: Get an eating-disorder evaluation plus a medical risk assessment.
Set up ongoing medical monitoring (vitals, labs, and safety checks as needed).
Identify which caregiver(s) will lead meal support and what supervision is realistic.
Create a simple, non-negotiable eating schedule (meals and snacks) with clear roles.
Start caregiver-led meal support immediately, with therapist coaching.
Reduce eating-disorder behaviors (restriction, compensatory exercise, purging) using practical supervision and limits.
Track safety and progress weekly and escalate care if medical or psychiatric risk rises.
As stability returns, gradually hand eating autonomy back to the adolescent with a relapse plan.
what_to_prepare: A brief symptom timeline (restriction, purging, exercise, weight changes, onset triggers)
Current medications, supplements, medical history, and clinician contact information
A realistic view of family schedules (school, work, meals, transportation)
A plan for supervision during high-risk times (after meals, evenings, weekends)
what_to_track: Meal completion and patterns of avoidance or negotiation
Purging, binge episodes, and compensatory exercise
Medical warning signs (dizziness, fainting, weakness) and when to seek urgent care
School attendance and functioning (energy, concentration, social withdrawal)
Caregiver burden and conflict levels (so supports can be added)

sections.preparation: A full assessment confirming diagnosis and determining safe level of care, with medical monitoring and a clear escalation plan.
procedure: Therapist-led family sessions that coach caregivers to take active responsibility for eating and symptom interruption
Phase 1: caregivers lead re-nourishment and reduce eating-disorder behaviors with consistent supervision
Phase 2: gradual return of age-appropriate control over eating to the adolescent as stability improves
Phase 3: relapse prevention, strengthening autonomy, and addressing developmental tasks and family patterns affected by the illness
sections.frequency: Often weekly early on, with spacing as stability improves.
sections.duration: Commonly 16–20 sessions over 6–12 months, adjusted to severity, risk, and response.

sections.pre_session: Review medical safety, eating patterns, and high-risk behaviors since last session; identify what worked and what broke down.
sections.treatment_phase: Coach caregivers on practical meal support, limit-setting, and reducing eating-disorder behaviors; troubleshoot barriers and align the family plan.
sections.post_session: Agree on specific next steps for supervision, routines, and supports; confirm when to escalate care if risk increases.

week_1: A strong focus on safety and nutrition first
Clear guidance that caregivers lead the eating plan temporarily
High emotion and resistance can show up quickly; the therapist helps families stay consistent without blame
week_4: More structured meal routines and clearer caregiver roles
Some symptoms may intensify as the disorder is challenged (arguing, bargaining, shutdown)
Families often need troubleshooting around school, social events, and supervision gaps
week_12: Improved consistency for many families, with fewer daily crises
Early steps toward returning autonomy if medical and behavioral stability is improving
More attention to sustaining routines and preventing slips during stress
signs_its_working: More consistent meal completion with less negotiation
Reduced eating-disorder behaviors (restriction, purging, compulsive exercise)
Improved energy, concentration, and day-to-day functioning
Caregivers feel more able to respond consistently without escalating conflict
signs_to_adjust: Ongoing weight loss or medical instability, or failure to stabilize eating behavior
Escalating purging or severe compulsive exercise
Increasing suicidality, self-harm, or inability to stay safe between sessions
If these occur, add supports and consider a higher level of care.

immediate: Clear structure for meals and supervision
Reduced confusion about roles and responsibilities
A safety plan that matches medical risk
short_term: Improved nutritional consistency and reduction in key behaviors for many patients
Better family coordination around meals and supervision
Improved daily functioning as nutrition stabilizes
long_term: Sustained symptom reduction and relapse prevention planning
Return of developmentally appropriate autonomy around eating
Improved family confidence in managing future flare-ups

mistakes: Waiting for the teen to be fully motivated before starting meal support
Arguing about logic or fairness during meals instead of following a plan
Inconsistent supervision (especially after meals or during weekends)
Treating FBT as “family blame” rather than a practical support method
Staying outpatient when medical or psychiatric risk clearly requires more care
fixes: Start with structure and consistency; motivation often improves after stability returns
Use short, calm statements and follow the plan; debrief later with the therapist
Identify supervision gaps and solve them with schedules, helpers, or program support
Keep the stance: the eating disorder is the problem; caregivers are allies
Escalate level of care promptly when safety criteria are not met

common: Increased anxiety and distress during early re-nourishment
More conflict at home as routines change
Short-term mood swings as nutrition and habits shift
rare: Worsening medical instability if intake remains inadequate (requires urgent medical review)
Caregiver burnout if support systems are not added early

concurrent_therapies: Medical monitoring with a clinician experienced in eating disorders
Dietitian support for meal planning and nutrition education
Psychiatry support when indicated for comorbid depression, anxiety, OCD, or sleep issues
Higher levels of care (IOP, PHP, residential, inpatient) when outpatient safety is not adequate
lifestyle_recommendations: Predictable meal and snack schedule with clear supervision
Temporarily limiting exercise if it is compulsive or medically risky
School coordination for meal support and reduced academic load when needed
Planned support for weekends, travel, and social events

sections.children: Often a strong fit when caregivers can supervise consistently and medical safety allows outpatient care.
sections.adolescents: Commonly used and often considered a first-line outpatient approach for anorexia nervosa in adolescents.
sections.cultural: FBT should be adapted to family structure, caregiving roles, food traditions, and privacy norms. The core goal is consistent nourishment with culturally appropriate support.

items.name: MANTRA (Maudsley Model for Adults)
items.how_its_different: MANTRA is designed for adults and focuses more on maintaining psychological and interpersonal factors, while FBT is caregiver-led and prioritizes rapid restoration of safe eating in youth.
items.when_that_might_be_better: MANTRA may fit better for adults living independently or when caregiver-led supervision is not feasible.

items.name: CBT-E (Enhanced CBT for Eating Disorders)
items.how_its_different: CBT-E is typically individual, skills- and behavior-focused across eating disorders; FBT is family-centered and uses caregivers to lead early behavior change for youth.
items.when_that_might_be_better: CBT-E may be preferred for adults, older adolescents who can self-manage safely, or when family involvement is not possible.

items.name: Adolescent-Focused Therapy (AFT)
items.how_its_different: AFT focuses more on individual adolescent work, autonomy, and emotion management; FBT relies more on caregiver-led meal support early on.
items.when_that_might_be_better: AFT may be considered when caregiver-led meal support is not workable, though outcomes depend on risk and engagement.

items.name: Higher Level of Care (PHP/Residential/Inpatient)
items.how_its_different: Programs provide structured meal supervision and medical/psychiatric monitoring multiple hours per day; FBT is outpatient and depends on home-based supervision.
items.when_that_might_be_better: A program is often better when there is medical instability, severe restriction, uncontrolled purging, or inability to stay safe at home.

what_feels_easy: Clear structure and expectations once the plan is set
Having caregivers take responsibility can reduce decision fatigue for the teen
Practical focus on meals can make early priorities feel concrete
what_feels_hard: Meals can become emotionally intense early on
Teens may feel a loss of control and react strongly
Caregivers may feel overwhelmed, guilty, or afraid of doing it wrong
Family conflict can spike before it improves
common_parent_or_patient_quotes: “We needed a clear plan, not more debates.”
“I hate it in the moment, but I don’t feel alone with this anymore.”
“Meals were the hardest part, but the structure helped.”
“It took teamwork and consistency, not perfect parenting.”

studies: Guidelines and reviews recommending FBT as a first-line outpatient treatment for adolescent anorexia nervosa.
Randomized trials comparing FBT with individual therapies for adolescent anorexia nervosa.
Evidence summaries supporting family-based approaches for adolescent bulimia nervosa in appropriate cases.
sections.limitations: FBT depends on caregiver availability, safe home supervision, and matching the level of care to medical and psychiatric risk. It is not appropriate when medical instability requires inpatient care or when home supervision is not feasible.

sections.typical_session_cost: Varies by region and provider; standard psychotherapy fees apply and may include multiple family members attending.
sections.total_treatment_cost: Moderate, often influenced by session count and need for dietitian and medical monitoring.
sections.insurance_coverage: Often covered under mental health benefits when medically necessary; coverage varies by plan and network status.
sections.cost_effectiveness: May reduce higher-cost care for some families when it prevents deterioration and supports early recovery, but depends on access, adherence, and risk level.

items.q: What is Family-Based Treatment (FBT) for eating disorders?
items.a: FBT is a structured therapy where caregivers temporarily take charge of helping a child or teen eat consistently and stop eating-disorder behaviors, with coaching from a trained clinician.

items.q: Is FBT the same as the Maudsley method?
items.a: FBT is often referred to as the Maudsley approach. Many people use the terms interchangeably, though services may vary in how closely they follow the manual.

items.q: Which eating disorders does FBT treat?
items.a: It is most strongly supported for adolescents with anorexia nervosa and is also used for adolescent bulimia nervosa in some settings when caregiver involvement is feasible.
No. The model treats the eating disorder as the problem. Caregivers are coached as allies to help restore health and stability.

items.q: Do parents have to force-feed their child?
items.a: FBT is not about force. It is about calm, consistent supervision and structured support so the teen can complete meals safely and reliably.
A typical course is often around 16–20 sessions over 6–12 months, but timelines vary with severity, medical risk, and response.

items.q: What happens in the three phases of FBT?
items.a: Phase 1 focuses on restoring safe eating with caregiver leadership, Phase 2 gradually returns control of eating to the adolescent as stability improves, and Phase 3 focuses on relapse prevention and normal development.

items.q: Can FBT be done if parents are divorced or there are multiple households?
items.a: Often yes, but it requires a clear plan for consistent supervision across homes. If coordination is not possible, additional supports may be needed.

items.q: Can FBT be done by telehealth?
items.a: Sometimes. It can work when the teen is medically stable, caregivers can supervise meals, and medical monitoring and escalation plans are in place.

items.q: What if my teen refuses to eat during FBT?
items.a: That is common early on. The therapist helps caregivers create a more effective structure and reduce negotiation. If refusal persists and safety worsens, a higher level of care may be needed.

items.q: Do we need a dietitian during FBT?
items.a: Many families benefit from dietitian support for meal planning and nutrition education, especially when fear foods, growth needs, or medical issues are involved.
If there is medical instability, uncontrolled purging, severe restriction that cannot be managed at home, or serious safety risk, a program level of care or inpatient stabilization may be necessary.

No. If there is immediate danger (fainting, chest pain, severe weakness, uncontrolled purging, or suicidal intent), seek urgent medical evaluation and contact local emergency services or your local emergency number.

items: FBT is commonly recommended as a first-line outpatient psychotherapy for adolescents with anorexia nervosa when medical stability allows.
The early phase prioritizes nutrition and symptom interruption; deeper psychological themes are usually addressed later once medical risk is lower.
Caregiver coaching is central; success often depends on consistency, supervision coverage, and rapid escalation when risk increases.
When home supervision is not possible or the environment is unsafe, alternative treatments or higher levels of care are more appropriate.

seo.title: Family-Based Treatment (FBT) for Adolescent Eating Disorders
seo.description: Family-Based Treatment (FBT) helps teens with anorexia nervosa (and some bulimia) restore eating with caregiver support; not for medical instability or emergencies.
